concepts.name: Fiscal Deficit: Definition and Precise Calculation
key_dimensions: Exact formula: Total Expenditure – Total Receipts excluding borrowings (NOT excluding all non-tax revenue)
Distinction between fiscal deficit and budget deficit (role of drawing down cash balances)
Why borrowings are excluded from receipts side — conceptual trap
Relationship to net RBI credit to government and monetisation

concepts.name: Components of Fiscal Deficit: Revenue vs Capital Dissection
key_dimensions: Fiscal Deficit = Revenue Deficit + Capital Expenditure – Net Capital Receipts (non-debt)
Implication: if revenue deficit is zero, fiscal deficit equals net capital spending — golden rule logic
UPSC trap: capital receipts include both debt and non-debt; only non-debt capital receipts offset capital expenditure
Disinvestment proceeds as non-debt capital receipt and its effect on fiscal deficit vs revenue deficit

concepts.name: Revenue Deficit vs Fiscal Deficit: Overlap and Divergence
key_dimensions: Revenue deficit = Revenue expenditure – Revenue receipts (entirely consumption-side measure)
A high revenue deficit embedded in fiscal deficit signals borrowing for consumption — intergenerational inequity argument
Effective Revenue Deficit: introduced in 2011-12 Union Budget — subtracts grants for capital asset creation
UPSC trap: Effective Revenue Deficit can be lower than Revenue Deficit but fiscal deficit remains unchanged

concepts.name: Primary Deficit: Meaning, Significance, and UPSC Traps
key_dimensions: Primary Deficit = Fiscal Deficit – Interest Payments (measures current policy stance excluding debt legacy)
A zero primary deficit means current revenue covers all non-interest expenditure — debt stabilisation condition
Primary deficit can be negative (primary surplus) even when fiscal deficit is positive — common MCQ trap
Use in assessing debt sustainability: Domar condition linkage (r vs g)

concepts.name: Fiscal Deficit Financing: Sources and Their Macroeconomic Consequences
key_dimensions: Market borrowings (G-Secs, T-Bills) vs small savings vs external borrowings vs RBI monetisation
Crowding-out effect: mechanism through interest rate channel vs availability channel
Monetisation of deficit: Ways and Means Advances (WMA) vs Open Market Operations (OMO) vs direct monetisation — distinctions
UPSC trap: WMA is temporary overdraft, NOT permanent monetisation; does not expand money supply permanently

concepts.name: Fiscal Responsibility and Budget Management (FRBM) Act, 2003: Targets and Amendments
key_dimensions: Original targets vs NK Singh Committee (2017) recommendations: 3% fiscal deficit, 1% revenue deficit, 40% debt-to-GDP
Escape clause (Section 4(3)): allows 0.5% deviation for national security, calamity, far-reaching structural reforms, decline in real output growth
UPSC trap: FRBM applies to Central Government only — states have separate fiscal responsibility acts
Suspension during COVID-19 and invocation of escape clause — recent factual relevance

concepts.name: NK Singh Committee Recommendations on FRBM Reform
key_dimensions: Shift from single fiscal deficit target to a Debt Rule (40% GDP for Centre, 20% for states by 2023) as the anchor
Fiscal deficit as instrument: 3% by 2020, with band of ±0.5%
Recommendation for independent Fiscal Council to provide non-binding forecasts — not yet implemented (UPSC trap)
Rejection of revenue deficit as primary target; preference for debt as nominal anchor

concepts.name: Fiscal Deficit and Inflation: Transmission Mechanisms
key_dimensions: Demand-pull channel: deficit-financed government spending raises aggregate demand
Monetisation channel: RBI financing deficit expands money supply directly
Distinction: bond-financed deficit is less inflationary than money-financed deficit in short run
UPSC trap: fiscal deficit does not always cause inflation — depends on output gap, method of financing, and import capacity

concepts.name: Fiscal Deficit and Current Account Deficit: Twin Deficit Hypothesis
key_dimensions: Mechanism: fiscal deficit → excess domestic demand → higher imports → current account deficit
National income identity linkage: (G–T) = (S–I) + (M–X) — Mundell-Fleming framework
Empirical limitations: twin deficits not always correlated in India — Ricardian Equivalence counterargument
UPSC trap: twin deficit is a hypothesis, not a law — India has had fiscal consolidation periods without current account surplus

concepts.name: Fiscal Deficit Targets in Indian Union Budgets: Trends and Deviations
key_dimensions: Pre-COVID consolidation path vs COVID year spike (9.3% in FY21) and glide path post-COVID
FY26 target of 4.5% and medium-term target of 4.5% — trajectory significance
Off-budget borrowings (NSSF loans to FCI, IEBR) understating true fiscal deficit — measurement controversy
UPSC trap: fiscal deficit as % of GDP can fall even if absolute deficit rises — denominator effect

concepts.name: Off-Budget Borrowings and True Fiscal Deficit Measurement
key_dimensions: Definition: borrowings by PSUs/special entities on government guarantee not reflected in Union Budget
Examples: Food Corporation of India borrowings from NSSF, NHAI bonds, Power sector bonds
CAG and NK Singh Committee criticism: off-budget items mask true fiscal stress
Government's 2021-22 move to bring FCI borrowings on-budget — apparent spike in deficit was statistical normalisation, not deterioration

concepts.name: Fiscal Deficit and Public Debt Sustainability: Domar Condition
key_dimensions: Domar condition: debt-to-GDP ratio stabilises when primary deficit/GDP = (g–r) × debt/GDP, where g = growth rate, r = interest rate
If r > g: even a primary surplus may not stabilise debt — dangerous spiral
India context: historically r < g has helped contain debt despite persistent deficits
UPSC trap: fiscal deficit and debt are related but not identical — stock vs flow distinction

concepts.name: Cyclical vs Structural Fiscal Deficit
key_dimensions: Cyclical component: automatic stabilisers (tax revenues fall, welfare spending rises in recession) — not a policy choice
Structural deficit: deficit that would exist at full employment/potential output — true measure of fiscal stance
India limitation: estimating output gap is contested, making structural deficit calculation imprecise
UPSC relevance: IMF and Finance Commission use structural measures; India's FRBM uses nominal targets — a known criticism

concepts.name: Fiscal Consolidation vs Fiscal Stimulus: Policy Trade-offs
key_dimensions: Expansionary austerity hypothesis (Alesina) vs Keynesian multiplier — empirical debate context
Composition matters: expenditure-based consolidation vs revenue-based consolidation — different growth impacts
Quality of fiscal deficit: capital-expenditure-driven deficit vs revenue-expenditure-driven deficit — crowding-in possibility
UPSC trap: reducing fiscal deficit is not always growth-positive — timing (recession vs boom) is critical

concepts.name: Finance Commission and Fiscal Deficit: Devolution-Deficit Linkage
key_dimensions: 15th Finance Commission's vertical devolution (41%) and its impact on Centre's fiscal space and net fiscal deficit
State fiscal deficit limits: 3% of GSDP under FRBM — states' borrowing permissions linked to Centre's conditions (power sector reforms)
Finance Commission grants vs devolution — only tax devolution reduces Centre's fiscal deficit (grants show as expenditure)
UPSC trap: increased devolution to states reduces Centre's fiscal deficit ceteris paribus but does not reduce general government deficit

concepts.name: General Government Deficit vs Central Government Deficit
key_dimensions: General Government = Centre + States + Union Territories with legislature
India's general government deficit consistently higher than Centre's alone — states' combined deficit adds ~2-3% of GDP
IMF uses general government deficit for cross-country comparisons — India often compared unfavourably when states included
UPSC trap: FRBM targets only Central Government fiscal deficit; no statutory consolidated general government target exists

concepts.name: Crowding Out Effect: Mechanism, Conditions, and Indian Evidence
key_dimensions: Financial crowding out: government borrowing raises interest rates → private investment declines
Physical crowding out: government competes for real resources (cement, steel) in a supply-constrained economy
Crowding IN: if government spends on infrastructure, it can raise private investment returns — complementarity argument
UPSC trap: crowding out is stronger when economy is at full employment; in a recession with slack, it may not occur — IS-LM logic

concepts.name: Fiscal Multiplier and Quality of Government Expenditure
key_dimensions: Fiscal multiplier > 1 when: economy has slack, monetary policy is accommodative, import leakage is low, Ricardian equivalence doesn't hold
Capital expenditure multiplier higher than revenue expenditure multiplier — empirical consensus
India-specific: NITI Aayog and RBI studies suggest multiplier around 1.5–2 for capital spending vs 0.9–1 for revenue spending
UPSC trap: a larger fiscal deficit does not always mean a larger stimulus — composition and financing method matter

concepts.name: Automatic Stabilisers vs Discretionary Fiscal Policy in Deficit Context
key_dimensions: Automatic stabilisers: progressive taxes, unemployment benefits — work without legislative action, dampen cyclical swings
India's limited automatic stabilisers: narrow tax base, weak social security — makes discretionary policy more important but also more prone to deficit bias
Deficit bias problem: political economy makes it easier to expand deficit than to reduce it — institutional solutions (FRBM, fiscal councils)
UPSC trap: India does not have unemployment insurance as a major automatic stabiliser unlike developed countries — MGNREGS is partial substitute but discretionary

concepts.name: Monetisation of Fiscal Deficit: Historical Context and Modern Constraints
key_dimensions: Pre-1997: ad hoc Treasury Bills — RBI automatically monetised deficit; abolished in April 1997
Post-1997: WMA (Ways and Means Advances) — short-term, collateralised, limited; RBI cannot directly subscribe to primary market G-Secs (FRBM 2003 provision)
COVID exception: RBI's OMOs and 'Operation Twist' — indirect monetisation through secondary market; distinction from direct monetisation
UPSC trap: RBI can purchase G-Secs in secondary market (OMO) — this is NOT prohibited; only primary market direct subscription is restricted under FRBM
